kits.familyName: Keeping commitments on a difficult morning
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}, and your shift starts at 8 a.m.
You are {role|a} at {workplace|a}. It is 7:30 a.m., and your shift starts at 8.
pressure: {coworker3} texts that the morning is going to be busy.
You know the team is short-staffed today.
detail: You packed your lunch the night before.

tiers.1: Your health and the health of others come first.
tiers.2: The team needs to know about a delay before the shift starts.
tiers.3: A missed commitment needs a new, realistic plan right away.
tiers.4: Repairing trust with a coworker you affected comes before discussing your own consequence.
tiers.5: Accepting a consequence well comes after the day's commitments are handled.

fact: You woke up with a fever, and the call-out policy says to call {lead|the} at least an hour before your shift.
issues.action: Call {lead|the} now, as the policy says, and stay home to recover.
issues.reason: Calling in early, as the policy asks, gives the lead time to find coverage, and staying home protects your coworkers.
issues.lesson: When you are sick, follow the call-out policy early so the team can plan.

shortcut.text: Come in anyway so nobody thinks you are unreliable.
shortcut.why: Working with a fever can spread illness and lower the quality of your work. Following the policy is the dependable choice.
shortcut.mis: Showing up no matter what is always the dependable choice.

fact: A traffic jam means you will reach work about 20 minutes after your shift starts.
clear: You already called {lead|the} to say you will be 20 minutes late.
issues.done: you already let {lead|the} know you will be late
issues.action: Let {lead|the} know right away that you will be about 20 minutes late.
issues.brief: tell {lead|the} you will be 20 minutes late
issues.reason: A quick warning lets the lead cover your duties until you arrive. Dependable people communicate before a problem, not after.
issues.lesson: If you will be late, tell your supervisor before your shift starts.

shortcut.text: Drive faster and hope to arrive close to on time.
shortcut.why: Rushing adds risk and may still leave you late with no warning given.
shortcut.mis: Making up time is better than admitting you will be late.

fact: The report you promised {lead|the} by yesterday afternoon is still not finished.
issues.action: Tell {lead|the} the report is not done and give a realistic finish time.
issues.brief: tell {lead|the} it is late and give a finish time
issues.reason: Admitting the miss and giving a realistic new time lets the lead plan. Silence leaves them guessing.
issues.lesson: When you miss a commitment, say so and set a realistic new one.

shortcut.text: Wait until {lead|the} asks about the report before mentioning it.
shortcut.why: Waiting to be asked hides the problem and makes it look like you hoped nobody would notice.
shortcut.mis: If nobody asks, a missed deadline does not need mentioning.

fact: An error you made yesterday caused {coworker} an hour of extra work this morning.
clear: You already apologized to {coworker} for yesterday's error.
issues.action: Own the error, apologize to {coworker}, and explain how you will prevent it.
issues.brief: own the error and apologize to {coworker}
issues.reason: Taking responsibility repairs trust, and a prevention plan shows the error will not repeat.
issues.lesson: Own your mistakes openly and show how you will prevent them.

shortcut.text: Say nothing, since {coworker} already fixed it.
shortcut.why: Staying quiet leaves your coworker feeling taken for granted and leaves the cause unaddressed.
shortcut.mis: Once a mistake is fixed, it is best not to bring it up.

fact: {Lead|the} told you that because of a late report last week, you will cover this Saturday's shift.
issues.short: the Saturday shift you were assigned
issues.action: Accept the Saturday shift and ask how to avoid the same problem in future.
issues.brief: accept Saturday and ask how to do better
issues.reason: Accepting a fair consequence without argument shows maturity, and asking how to improve turns it into progress.
issues.lesson: Accept fair consequences calmly and use them to improve.

shortcut.text: Argue that the late report was not really your fault.
shortcut.brief: argue it was not your fault
shortcut.why: Arguing about a consequence for a real lapse damages trust. Accepting it and improving builds it back.
shortcut.mis: Arguing a consequence shows you care about fairness.

proceed.text: Start your shift as planned and work through your task list.
proceed.why: Nothing in the situation needs extra attention, so the dependable move is to start on time and get to work.
proceed.lesson: Dependability is mostly showing up ready and doing the work as planned.

generic.text: Blame the busy schedule when {lead|the} asks about any problems.
generic.why: Blaming circumstances avoids responsibility and does not fix anything.
generic.mis: Explaining a problem away is the same as dealing with it.

generic.text: Take an extra-long break later to make up for the stressful morning.
generic.why: A stressful morning does not change your schedule. Extra break time leaves the team short.
generic.mis: A hard morning earns extra time off.

overcaution.text: Call {lead|the} to confirm your schedule again before you leave home.
overcaution.why: Nothing in the situation calls for a check-in. Calling to confirm a known schedule takes the lead's time for no reason.
overcaution.mis: Checking in more always shows dependability.

setup: You are {role|a} at {workplace|a}, getting ready for a shift that starts at 8 a.m.

late: You realize you will not make it in time for the start of your shift.
overdue: A report you promised {lead|the} is past due.
mistake: Your error yesterday made extra work for {coworker}.

rel: The warning only helps if it comes before you arrive late.
You review the list once you are at work.
An in-person apology happens once you are there.
Looking at the day's tasks shows when the report can realistically be finished.
The lead should know the new deadline before you dive into other work.
You need to know the day's tasks before starting them.
process.lesson: Communicate early, show up, plan the day, and repair any missed commitments.

title: Your message to {lead|the}
intro: You are about to email {lead|the} about the overdue report. Check the message first.
doc.lesson: Accountable messages admit the problem, avoid excuses and blame, and give a realistic plan.

lines.text: I did not finish the report by yesterday afternoon as I promised.

bad.text: The report is late because {coworker} never sent me the numbers on time.
bad.why: Blaming a coworker avoids responsibility, especially when the commitment was yours.

lines.text: I underestimated how long the second section would take.
lines.fine: Gives an honest reason without excuses.

lines.text: I will have it to you by 2 p.m. today.

bad.text: I will try to get it to you sometime soon.
bad.why: A vague promise does not let the lead plan. A specific, realistic time is needed.

lines.text: I have two hours free this morning to work on it.
lines.fine: Shows the new deadline is realistic.

lines.text: That leaves time to check it before I send it.
lines.fine: Plans for quality, not just speed.

bad.text: I will finish all of it in the next 20 minutes, and you can have it by 8:30.
bad.why: The message says the work needs about two hours and promises 2 p.m. A 20-minute promise contradicts both and will likely be missed.

lines.text: Next time I will check in with you as soon as I see a deadline slipping.
lines.fine: Explains how the problem will be prevented.

bad.text: These things happen, so I would not worry about it.
bad.why: Brushing off a missed commitment suggests it will happen again. A prevention plan shows accountability.

review.notes: Call-out timing is stated as workplace policy. Sick state is beginner-only because it replaces the rest of the day.

kits.familyName: Keeping quality up on repetitive work
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}, finishing a large batch of similar work today. Each piece needs a final check.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are working through a long, repetitive batch, and each piece must be checked before it moves on.
pressure: {coworker3} says nobody ever looks closely at this work anyway.
The daily target is posted on the board.
detail: You are about halfway through the batch.
The work area is quiet this afternoon.

tiers.1: A required check is part of the job, not an optional extra.
tiers.2: Work you know is flawed must not move on.
tiers.3: You cannot check against a standard you are unsure about.
tiers.4: A missed target should be explained, not hidden by rushing.
tiers.5: Managing your focus matters, but not ahead of real quality problems.

fact: {coworker} shows you how to skip the final check to finish the batch much faster.
issues.short: the shortcut that skips the final check
issues.action: Keep doing the final check on every piece, as the procedure requires.
issues.reason: The check is there because errors happen. Skipping it puts the quality of the whole batch at risk.
issues.lesson: Diligence means doing every required step, even when a shortcut is offered.

shortcut.text: Skip the check on the simple pieces to save time.
shortcut.brief: skip the check on simple pieces
shortcut.why: Simple pieces can still have errors. The procedure requires the check on every piece.
shortcut.mis: Easy work does not need checking.

fact: You discover that several pieces you finished earlier all have the same flaw.
issues.action: Set the flawed pieces aside, fix them, and tell {lead|the} what happened.
issues.brief: set aside and fix the flawed pieces
issues.reason: Holding back flawed work protects the next person in line, and telling the lead lets them check for a wider problem.
issues.lesson: When you find flaws in your own work, stop them, fix them and say so.

shortcut.text: Send the pieces along, since the next person will probably catch it.
shortcut.why: Passing on work you know is flawed shifts your responsibility to someone else and risks it reaching a {client}.
shortcut.mis: Someone further along will catch the problem.

fact: You are not sure whether a small scratch counts as a defect.
clear: {Lead|the} showed you this morning exactly which scratches count as defects.
issues.done: you were already shown the standard for scratches
issues.action: Ask {lead|the} what the standard is for small scratches.
issues.reason: You cannot check work properly against a standard you are unsure of. A quick question makes every check reliable.
issues.lesson: Know the quality standard before you judge your work against it.

shortcut.text: Decide for yourself that small scratches do not matter.
shortcut.why: Guessing at the standard may let defects through or waste good pieces. The lead can tell you.
shortcut.mis: Your own judgment is the standard.

fact: You are behind the daily target because a tricky piece took extra care.
clear: {Lead|the} already knows you are behind and said quality comes first.
issues.action: Tell {lead|the} you are behind and why, while keeping the quality up.
issues.brief: tell {lead|the} you are behind and why
issues.reason: The lead can adjust plans if they know. Rushing to hide the gap would trade quality for appearances.
issues.lesson: Explain a missed target honestly instead of rushing to hide it.

shortcut.text: Rush the rest so the count looks right by the end of the day.
shortcut.brief: rush the rest to hit the count
shortcut.why: Rushing invites errors in the remaining work. Explaining the delay is better than hiding it.
shortcut.mis: Hitting the number matters more than how the work is done.

fact: The work is repetitive, and you notice your attention starting to drift.
issues.action: Take your scheduled break now, then come back and refocus on each piece.
issues.reason: Drifting attention is when errors creep in. A scheduled break restores focus without skipping any work.
issues.lesson: Notice when your focus slips and use breaks to stay careful.

shortcut.text: Watch videos on your phone while you work to stay awake.
shortcut.why: Splitting attention makes errors more likely, not less.
shortcut.mis: Distractions help you get through boring work.

proceed.text: Keep working steadily through the batch, checking each piece.
proceed.why: Nothing in the situation needs attention, so steady, careful work is what the job calls for.
proceed.lesson: Diligent work is steady, careful and complete, even when it is repetitive.

generic.text: Ask {coworker2} to check your pieces for you while you take a break.
generic.why: The checks are your responsibility. Handing them off adds to a coworker's load without reason.
generic.mis: Responsibility for quality can be passed to whoever is free.

generic.text: Mark the batch as finished now and complete the last pieces tomorrow.
generic.why: Recording unfinished work as finished makes the record false.
generic.mis: It is fine to report work as done if you plan to finish it.

overcaution.text: Ask {lead|the} to inspect every piece before you continue.
overcaution.why: Nothing in the situation calls for an extra inspection. It would stall the batch and take the lead's time.
overcaution.mis: Supervisor checks are always better than your own.

setup: You are {role|a} at {workplace|a}, working through a large batch where each piece is checked before it moves on.

standard: You are unsure what counts as a defect.
flaw: Some pieces from earlier turned out to share a flaw.

steps.text: Ask {lead|the} which scratches count as defects
Inspect the piece against the standard
Pull aside any piece that fails
Record the piece in the batch count

rel: You need the standard before you can inspect against it.
A piece is inspected once it is finished.
Only an inspection shows which pieces fail.
Failed pieces are pulled before the count is recorded.
Only inspected pieces go into the count.
process.lesson: Know the standard, finish, inspect, hold back failures, then record the count.

title: End-of-day batch report
intro: You are about to hand {lead|the} this batch report. Check it first.
doc.lesson: An accountable report is accurate about what was done, checked and held back.

lines.fine: States the result honestly against the target.

lines.text: All 120 pieces received the final check.
lines.fine: Confirms the required step was done.

bad.text: I skipped the final check on the simple pieces to save time.
bad.why: The check is required on every piece. Skipping it puts quality at risk.

lines.text: Six pieces had the same flaw and are set aside for rework.

bad.text: Six pieces had a flaw, but I sent them on, since the next station usually catches problems.
bad.why: Known flaws should be held back, not passed on for someone else to catch.

lines.text: I fell behind because one piece needed extra care.
That leaves 114 good pieces ready to move on.

bad.text: That leaves all 120 pieces ready to move on.
bad.why: Six of the 120 were set aside for rework, so only 114 are ready. The total contradicts the report.

lines.text: I will finish the last 30 tomorrow morning.
lines.fine: Gives a plan for the remaining work.

bad.text: I marked the batch finished so the board looks right; the last 30 can wait.
bad.why: Marking unfinished work as finished makes the record false.

review.notes: Diligence and accountability; numbers in the report are internally consistent (120 - 6 = 114).
